Outside of that, though, I don't really experience any generalized dread or excessive worry about other everyday areas of my life.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how long these feelings of emotional heaviness and difficulty with decision-making have been affecting you, and have they been constant or do they fluctuate?\n\nPatient: This current low spell has been pretty constant for about three months now, ever since the most intense phase of our project rollout started. My coworkers joked I was on \"1.5x speed\" because I talked so fast and wouldn't let others speak, and I would snap at people over minor delays. While I definitely felt overly confident, slept very little, and took on way too much, my focus was entirely on over-committing to work projects and initiatives rather than doing anything dangerous or out of character.\n\nDoctor: During your high episodes, have you ever experienced an increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, such as feeling like you're constantly 'on the go' or having an inability to relax, in addition to your feelings of excitement and reduced need for sleep?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. While coworkers noticed I was moving at \"1.5x speed\" and could be irritable, those phases felt manageable and didn't cause functional failure. The real impairment and distress only hit when I crashed into the low periods, and it is this unpredictable cycle of highs and lows that has finally disrupted my ability to function at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether you have experienced at least one major depressive episode in addition to your hypomanic episodes, or have your episodes been primarily hypomanic with depressive episodes that do not meet the full criteria for a major depressive episode?\n\nPatient: Yes, I have absolutely experienced full, severe depressive episodes, and this current three-month crash has been completely debilitating. My mind is wrapped in a total fog that leaves me completely unable to make basic decisions at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there has ever been a period where you experienced both depressive and hypomanic symptoms either simultaneously or in rapid succession, without a clear switch between the two, and if so, how did that affect your daily functioning?"

During those times, I actually feel highly capable, energetic, and overly productive, though my coworkers notice me talking and moving at \"1.5x speed.\" The severe impairment and disruption to my work only occur when I crash into these low, depressive periods.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any high episodes that lasted less than four days, and if so, how did they differ from your typical week-long high episodes in terms of intensity and impact on your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, as I haven't noticed any high episodes that short. My high periods usually seem to last at least a week or more, and I haven't tracked them closely enough to compare or notice any shorter shifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm that your high episodes, which typically last about a week or two, have never required hospitalization or caused significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, but rather made you feel highly capable and productive?\n\nPatient: Yes, that's correct; I've never needed hospital visits, and those highs actually made me feel incredibly capable and confident, like I could single-handedly turn the whole division around. I would sleep very little but feel totally fine while packing my schedule with extra projects. The real impairment and struggle only started when I crashed into this current low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever met the full criteria for a hypomanic episode, such as lasting at least four consecutive days, or have they always been shorter or less severe?\n\nPatient: Yes, my high episodes definitely last longer than four days, and my most recent one actually lasted for a couple of weeks before I crashed. During that entire stretch, I felt constantly buzzing with excitement, slept very little, and was highly active. It was definitely a sustained, continuous period rather than just a fleeting couple of days.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode that lasted longer than four days but was severe enough to cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning, or have all your high episodes been less severe and not caused significant impairment?\n\nPatient: No, none of my high episodes have ever caused significant impairment on their own, even though they last a couple of weeks and make me feel highly energetic and productive. During those times I felt like I was doing great, even if coworkers noticed me talking fast or being a bit irritable. The actual impairment, missed deadlines, and severe struggle at work only happen when I crash into these low, foggy periods.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance during your high episodes where your behavior was so erratic or out of character that it caused problems in your relationships or at work, even if you didn't feel impaired yourself?\n\nPatient: Yes, my behavior definitely raised some eyebrows and caused friction with my team during those high periods. My coworkers joked I was on \"1.5x speed\" because I talked so fast and wouldn't let others speak, and I would snap at people over minor delays. I also had this mindset that I was the only one who really understood the project, which created a lot of tension.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode where you had psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, or where you engaged in risky behaviors that had significant consequences, such as excessive spending or reckless decisions?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never experienced anything like hallucinations or delusions, and I haven't engaged in risky behaviors like reckless spending or dangerous decisions. While I definitely felt overly confident, slept very little, and took on way too much, my focus was entirely on over-committing to work projects and initiatives rather than doing anything dangerous or out of character.\n\nDoctor: During your high episodes, have you ever experienced an increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, such as feeling like you're constantly 'on the go' or having an inability to relax, in addition to your feelings of excitement and reduced need for sleep?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. During those highs, I had this restless drive where I couldn't sit still, packing my calendar with extra plant visits, meetings, and side projects all at once. I felt constantly \"on the go\" and couldn't switch off, even pacing my hotel room at midnight planning new initiatives because it was just impossible to relax.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever caused significant distress or impairment in your social or occupational functioning, or have they always been manageable and not interfered with your daily life?\n\nPatient: During those high periods, I didn't feel distressed or impaired at all—I actually felt extremely productive, energized, and on top of the world, chalking it up to normal project cycles. While coworkers noticed I was moving at \"1.5x speed\" and could be irritable, those phases felt manageable and didn't cause functional failure. The real impairment and distress only hit when I crashed into the low periods, and it is this unpredictable cycle of highs and lows that has finally disrupted my ability to function at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether you have experienced at least one major depressive episode in addition to your hypomanic episodes, or have your episodes been primarily hypomanic with depressive episodes that do not meet the full criteria for a major depressive episode?\n\nPatient: Yes, I have absolutely experienced full, severe depressive episodes, and this current three-month crash has been completely debilitating. I feel utterly hollow and tearful, have lost my appetite entirely, and struggle with severe insomnia while moving so slowly that everything takes immense physical effort. My mind is wrapped in a total fog that leaves me completely unable to make basic decisions at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there has ever been a period where you experienced both depressive and hypomanic symptoms either simultaneously or in rapid succession, without a clear switch between the two, and if so, how did that affect your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced both high and low symptoms at the exact same time or switched rapidly back and forth without a break. Instead, my experiences have always felt like distinct, separate phases. I'll have a clear period of high energy and drive, which is then followed by a very noticeable crash into a low, sluggish state.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt abnormally elevated or irritable, with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and increased activity, and if so, did this period cause significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning?"

It’s like I'm constantly stuck trying to wade through my own thoughts.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing excessive worry or fear about everyday things, such as your performance at work or other aspects of your life, that's out of proportion to the actual situation?\n\nPatient: I definitely worry about my work performance right now, but that's because I'm genuinely struggling and making mistakes on the job. Outside of that, though, I don't really experience any generalized dread or excessive worry about other everyday areas of my life.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how long these feelings of emotional heaviness and difficulty with decision-making have been affecting you, and have they been constant or do they fluctuate?\n\nPatient: This current low spell has been pretty constant for about three months now, ever since the most intense phase of our project rollout started. But looking back, I've actually been cycling through these kinds of highs and crashes since my mid-twenties. It's just that over the past year, the pattern has become much more severe and impossible for me and my coworkers to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe the nature and duration of your 'highs' - do you experience periods of abnormally elevated mood, increased energy, or reduced need for sleep, and if so, how long do these episodes typically last?\n\nPatient: During those high periods, which usually last a week or two, I feel buzzing with excitement, talk at \"1.5x speed,\" and pack my schedule with constant activity while sleeping only three or four hours a night without feeling tired. I can also become irrationally irritable and snap at people, and while I've cycled through these highs and crashes since my mid-twenties, they have become much more intense over the past year.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many of these high and low episodes you've experienced in the past year, and have you noticed any pattern or trigger that seems to precede the shift from one episode to another?\n\nPatient: Over the past year, these cycles have become much more frequent and intense due to the constant pressure of my new project. Most recently, a highly energetic, buzzing \"up\" phase that lasted about two weeks immediately triggered this current \"low\" crash, which has been dragging on for three months now. The main triggers seem to be chronic sleep deprivation, intense work pressure, and over-committing myself during those high phases, which always seems to push me from one extreme to the other.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your high episodes have ever lasted longer than a few weeks, or if they've ever been severe enough to cause significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, such as requiring hospitalization?\n\nPatient: No, those high phases have never lasted longer than a couple of weeks, and I've never needed hospitalization or felt impaired during them—in fact, I felt overly capable and took on tons of extra work. The severe struggle and impairment at work only happen when I crash into these low, depressive phases.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode that lasted longer than four days but less than two weeks and was not severe enough to cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning, or have all your high episodes been either shorter or more severe?\n\nPatient: Yes, my high episodes typically last about a week or two and do not cause any impairment. During those times, I actually feel highly capable, energetic, and overly productive, though my coworkers notice me talking and moving at \"1.5x speed.\" The severe impairment and disruption to my work only occur when I crash into these low, depressive periods.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any high episodes that lasted less than four days, and if so, how did they differ from your typical week-long high episodes in terms of intensity and impact on your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, as I haven't noticed any high episodes that short. My high periods usually seem to last at least a week or more, and I haven't tracked them closely enough to compare or notice any shorter shifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm that your high episodes, which typically last about a week or two, have never required hospitalization or caused significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, but rather made you feel highly capable and productive?\n\nPatient: Yes, that's correct; I've never needed hospital visits, and those highs actually made me feel incredibly capable and confident, like I could single-handedly turn the whole division around. I would sleep very little but feel totally fine while packing my schedule with extra projects. The real impairment and struggle only started when I crashed into this current low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever met the full criteria for a hypomanic episode, such as lasting at least four consecutive days, or have they always been shorter or less severe?\n\nPatient: Yes, my high episodes definitely last longer than four days, and my most recent one actually lasted for a couple of weeks before I crashed. During that entire stretch, I felt constantly buzzing with excitement, slept very little, and was highly active. It was definitely a sustained, continuous period rather than just a fleeting couple of days.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode that lasted longer than four days but was severe enough to cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning, or have all your high episodes been less severe and not caused significant impairment?\n\nPatient: No, none of my high episodes have ever caused significant impairment on their own, even though they last a couple of weeks and make me feel highly energetic and productive. During those times I felt like I was doing great, even if coworkers noticed me talking fast or being a bit irritable. The actual impairment, missed deadlines, and severe struggle at work only happen when I crash into these low, foggy periods.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance during your high episodes where your behavior was so erratic or out of character that it caused problems in your relationships or at work, even if you didn't feel impaired yourself?\n\nPatient: Yes, my behavior definitely raised some eyebrows and caused friction with my team during those high periods. My coworkers joked I was on \"1.5x speed\" because I talked so fast and wouldn't let others speak, and I would snap at people over minor delays. I also had this mindset that I was the only one who really understood the project, which created a lot of tension.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode where you had psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, or where you engaged in risky behaviors that had significant consequences, such as excessive spending or reckless decisions?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never experienced anything like hallucinations or delusions, and I haven't engaged in risky behaviors like reckless spending or dangerous decisions. While I definitely felt overly confident, slept very little, and took on way too much, my focus was entirely on over-committing to work projects and initiatives rather than doing anything dangerous or out of character.\n\nDoctor: During your high episodes, have you ever experienced an increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, such as feeling like you're constantly 'on the go' or having an inability to relax, in addition to your feelings of excitement and reduced need for sleep?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. During those highs, I had this restless drive where I couldn't sit still, packing my calendar with extra plant visits, meetings, and side projects all at once. I felt constantly \"on the go\" and couldn't switch off, even pacing my hotel room at midnight planning new initiatives because it was just impossible to relax.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever caused significant distress or impairment in your social or occupational functioning, or have they always been manageable and not interfered with your daily life?\n\nPatient: During those high periods, I didn't feel distressed or impaired at all—I actually felt extremely productive, energized, and on top of the world, chalking it up to normal project cycles. While coworkers noticed I was moving at \"1.5x speed\" and could be irritable, those phases felt manageable and didn't cause functional failure. The real impairment and distress only hit when I crashed into the low periods, and it is this unpredictable cycle of highs and lows that has finally disrupted my ability to function at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether you have experienced at least one major depressive episode in addition to your hypomanic episodes, or have your episodes been primarily hypomanic with depressive episodes that do not meet the full criteria for a major depressive episode?\n\nPatient: Yes, I have absolutely experienced full, severe depressive episodes, and this current three-month crash has been completely debilitating. I feel utterly hollow and tearful, have lost my appetite entirely, and struggle with severe insomnia while moving so slowly that everything takes immense physical effort. My mind is wrapped in a total fog that leaves me completely unable to make basic decisions at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there has ever been a period where you experienced both depressive and hypomanic symptoms either simultaneously or in rapid succession, without a clear switch between the two, and if so, how did that affect your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced both high and low symptoms at the exact same time or switched rapidly back and forth without a break. Instead, my experiences have always felt like distinct, separate phases. I'll have a clear period of high energy and drive, which is then followed by a very noticeable crash into a low, sluggish state.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt abnormally elevated or irritable, with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and increased activity, and if so, did this period cause significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've had those high, irritable periods lasting a couple of weeks, which has been a pattern cycling since my mid-twenties. In those phases, I was buzzing with energy, sleeping only three to four hours a night, speaking incredibly fast, and taking on excessive tasks. I felt overly confident and highly productive despite snapping at coworkers, so the real impairment and threat to my job only occurred when I crashed into my current low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the total number of distinct hypomanic and major depressive episodes you've experienced in the past year, and have you noticed any consistent pattern or cycle between these episodes?\n\nPatient: It's hard to give an exact number of episodes because I always wrote them off as normal ups and downs of my work cycles, though I've noticed this pattern since my mid-twenties. I consistently cycle from weeks of high-octane brainstorming and socializing straight into these heavy crashes where everything feels like wading through mud. This past year the pattern became impossible to ignore, with my current low lasting about three months immediately following a buzzing, two-week high phase.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted less than four days but were still noticeable, or have all your high episodes been longer and more pronounced?"

All of my high episodes have been longer and more pronounced, usually stretching over weeks rather than just a few days. For instance, the buzzing phase I experienced right before this current crash lasted for about a couple of weeks. I really haven't noticed any of those high-energy periods lasting less than four days.

During those times, I actually feel highly capable, energetic, and overly productive, though my coworkers notice me talking and moving at \"1.5x speed.\" The severe impairment and disruption to my work only occur when I crash into these low, depressive periods.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any high episodes that lasted less than four days, and if so, how did they differ from your typical week-long high episodes in terms of intensity and impact on your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, as I haven't noticed any high episodes that short. My high periods usually seem to last at least a week or more, and I haven't tracked them closely enough to compare or notice any shorter shifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm that your high episodes, which typically last about a week or two, have never required hospitalization or caused significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning, but rather made you feel highly capable and productive?\n\nPatient: Yes, that's correct; I've never needed hospital visits, and those highs actually made me feel incredibly capable and confident, like I could single-handedly turn the whole division around. I would sleep very little but feel totally fine while packing my schedule with extra projects. The real impairment and struggle only started when I crashed into this current low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever met the full criteria for a hypomanic episode, such as lasting at least four consecutive days, or have they always been shorter or less severe?\n\nPatient: Yes, my high episodes definitely last longer than four days, and my most recent one actually lasted for a couple of weeks before I crashed. During that entire stretch, I felt constantly buzzing with excitement, slept very little, and was highly active. It was definitely a sustained, continuous period rather than just a fleeting couple of days.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode that lasted longer than four days but was severe enough to cause significant impairment in social or occupational functioning, or have all your high episodes been less severe and not caused significant impairment?\n\nPatient: No, none of my high episodes have ever caused significant impairment on their own, even though they last a couple of weeks and make me feel highly energetic and productive. During those times I felt like I was doing great, even if coworkers noticed me talking fast or being a bit irritable. The actual impairment, missed deadlines, and severe struggle at work only happen when I crash into these low, foggy periods.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instance during your high episodes where your behavior was so erratic or out of character that it caused problems in your relationships or at work, even if you didn't feel impaired yourself?\n\nPatient: Yes, my behavior definitely raised some eyebrows and caused friction with my team during those high periods. My coworkers joked I was on \"1.5x speed\" because I talked so fast and wouldn't let others speak, and I would snap at people over minor delays. I also had this mindset that I was the only one who really understood the project, which created a lot of tension.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a high episode where you had psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, or where you engaged in risky behaviors that had significant consequences, such as excessive spending or reckless decisions?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never experienced anything like hallucinations or delusions, and I haven't engaged in risky behaviors like reckless spending or dangerous decisions. While I definitely felt overly confident, slept very little, and took on way too much, my focus was entirely on over-committing to work projects and initiatives rather than doing anything dangerous or out of character.\n\nDoctor: During your high episodes, have you ever experienced an increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, such as feeling like you're constantly 'on the go' or having an inability to relax, in addition to your feelings of excitement and reduced need for sleep?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. During those highs, I had this restless drive where I couldn't sit still, packing my calendar with extra plant visits, meetings, and side projects all at once. I felt constantly \"on the go\" and couldn't switch off, even pacing my hotel room at midnight planning new initiatives because it was just impossible to relax.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your high episodes have ever caused significant distress or impairment in your social or occupational functioning, or have they always been manageable and not interfered with your daily life?\n\nPatient: During those high periods, I didn't feel distressed or impaired at all—I actually felt extremely productive, energized, and on top of the world, chalking it up to normal project cycles. While coworkers noticed I was moving at \"1.5x speed\" and could be irritable, those phases felt manageable and didn't cause functional failure. The real impairment and distress only hit when I crashed into the low periods, and it is this unpredictable cycle of highs and lows that has finally disrupted my ability to function at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether you have experienced at least one major depressive episode in addition to your hypomanic episodes, or have your episodes been primarily hypomanic with depressive episodes that do not meet the full criteria for a major depressive episode?\n\nPatient: Yes, I have absolutely experienced full, severe depressive episodes, and this current three-month crash has been completely debilitating. I feel utterly hollow and tearful, have lost my appetite entirely, and struggle with severe insomnia while moving so slowly that everything takes immense physical effort. My mind is wrapped in a total fog that leaves me completely unable to make basic decisions at work.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there has ever been a period where you experienced both depressive and hypomanic symptoms either simultaneously or in rapid succession, without a clear switch between the two, and if so, how did that affect your daily functioning?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced both high and low symptoms at the exact same time or switched rapidly back and forth without a break. Instead, my experiences have always felt like distinct, separate phases. I'll have a clear period of high energy and drive, which is then followed by a very noticeable crash into a low, sluggish state.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt abnormally elevated or irritable, with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and increased activity, and if so, did this period cause significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've had those high, irritable periods lasting a couple of weeks, which has been a pattern cycling since my mid-twenties. In those phases, I was buzzing with energy, sleeping only three to four hours a night, speaking incredibly fast, and taking on excessive tasks. I felt overly confident and highly productive despite snapping at coworkers, so the real impairment and threat to my job only occurred when I crashed into my current low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the total number of distinct hypomanic and major depressive episodes you've experienced in the past year, and have you noticed any consistent pattern or cycle between these episodes?\n\nPatient: It's hard to give an exact number of episodes because I always wrote them off as normal ups and downs of my work cycles, though I've noticed this pattern since my mid-twenties. I consistently cycle from weeks of high-octane brainstorming and socializing straight into these heavy crashes where everything feels like wading through mud. This past year the pattern became impossible to ignore, with my current low lasting about three months immediately following a buzzing, two-week high phase.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted less than four days but were still noticeable, or have all your high episodes been longer and more pronounced?\n\nPatient: All of my high episodes have been longer and more pronounced, usually stretching over weeks rather than just a few days. For instance, the buzzing phase I experienced right before this current crash lasted for about a couple of weeks. I really haven't noticed any of those high-energy periods lasting less than four days.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your current depressive episode, which has lasted for three months, is the longest you've experienced, or have you had longer depressive episodes in the past?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that this current low spell has been going on for about three months now. However, I'm not entirely sure of the exact duration of my past low episodes, or whether any of them lasted longer than this one. Since I used to just write them off as normal reactions to my work cycles, I never tracked their length very closely.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of more than two weeks where you experienced both depressive and manic or hypomanic symptoms simultaneously, or did you always experience a clear switch between the high and low episodes?\n\nPatient: It has always felt like a clear switch for me rather than experiencing both states at the same time. I typically have a distinct high period of intense energy and buzzing activity, which is then followed by a distinct crash into a heavy, foggy low period.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods of hypomania that lasted less than four consecutive days but were still noticeable, or have all your hypomanic episodes lasted at least four days?"
